title: Pooling three visits gave no clear relative warmth slope change for two frogs in four US samples in 2001-2015
abstract: We tested whether pooling three seasonal visits changes spring warmth slopes for recorded frog presence. We used wood frog and green frog records in the Northeast and Midwest US in 2001-2008 and 2009-2015. Each stop-year had three ordered visits by one observer at one stop. The eight models used 39,397 species-stop-year records, with overlap between species. We compared annual any detection with mean detection per visit, after scaling each slope by its index mean. All eight paired differences had 95 percent and eight-test adjusted intervals that included zero. Estimates ranged from -2.81 to +0.51 percentage points of relative response per C. All planned sensitivity intervals included zero. An exact index relation shows that the normalized indices are equal when a detected year has only one positive visit. Repeat detections occurred in only 2.0-2.5 percent of positive wood frog stop-years. These data show no clear common change in relative slopes from this pooling rule. They do not show that either index measures occupancy without bias. Few year clusters, selected complete schedules, coarse weather and shared observations limit inference. Code, checked histories, source hashes and raw retrieval steps support reproduction. Air pollution and daily extremes were not tested.

display.caption: Relative warmth slopes and paired annual detection minus mean-visit contrasts. Two frogs, two US regions and two periods. Thick lines show 95 percent limits. Thin lines show eight-test adjusted limits. All primary limits include zero. The indices use identical stop visits and observers.
